text: Everything modeled so far has come from traditional sources: prices, volumes, fundamentals, filings, news. Alternative data steps outside that entirely, and it's one of the most talked-about edges in modern quantitative finance, and also one of the hardest to use responsibly.

The main categories include satellite imagery, used to count cars in parking lots or track oil tanker drafts; anonymized credit-card transaction panels that can estimate a retailer's sales weeks before earnings; web-scraped pricing across e-commerce sites; social media chatter around a brand or ticker; shipping and supply-chain data like vessel tracking; and geolocation data estimating store visits or regional activity.

The appeal is real: if a data source reveals a company's actual performance before it shows up in a filing or a price move, a model trained on it has a genuine head start. But that edge is inherently temporary, because as more funds discover and license the same dataset, more capital trades on the same signal and the price impact erodes it, the same way any discovered inefficiency gets arbitraged away. On top of that, most alternative datasets are commercially new, often only two or three years of clean history, which simply isn't enough for the kind of robust, multi-regime validation this course has emphasized.

Vendor quality is its own problem. Coverage gaps and shifting panel composition can masquerade as a market trend when it's really just a change in the underlying sample. Survivorship bias is a particular risk: a vendor might backfill coverage for companies that still exist today while never including ones that went bankrupt, which flatters a historical backtest. And legally, not every data source is fair game. Material non-public information, or MNPI, is illegal to trade on regardless of how it was obtained, so any new alternative data source needs a real compliance review before it reaches a model.
A new data source is one frontier. Up next, lesson twenty-five: reinforcement learning for trading, a look at a still-emerging approach to the learning problem itself.
